My grandmother listened to the same local radio programme every Sunday. One week, a cook described a soup that Grandma wanted to try. She wrote down the ingredients, but the radio signal (1) ____ before the cook explained how long to heat the soup. All we could hear was a rough noise.

“I remember the name of the programme,” she said. “Perhaps we can find it online.” I searched and found a recording. We listened to the last part again. Grandma added the missing (2) ____ to her notes: fifteen minutes, not fifty.

The following morning, I helped her prepare the vegetables. She cut the carrots into small pieces and asked me to measure the water. I almost poured it straight into the pot. “Use the jug,” she said. “We need to know the (3) ____.” The marks on its side showed the number of millilitres.

While the soup was heating, Grandma told me that she used to follow recipes from magazines. Radio was useful, but written instructions were easier to (4) ____ while cooking. I suggested printing the online recipe. She agreed, provided that we used a large font so she could read it without her glasses.

When we tasted the soup, we both found it too salty. I felt the whole morning had been (5) ____, but Grandma laughed. “We have a meal, and we know what to change.” She crossed out “one spoon of salt” and wrote “half a spoon” in its (6) ____. Then she dated the page. The recipe was no longer an order we had to follow (7) ____. It was a starting point for a meal that would suit (8) ____.

completed_passage:
My grandmother listened to the same local radio programme every Sunday. One week, a cook described a soup that Grandma wanted to try. She wrote down the ingredients, but the radio signal failed before the cook explained how long to heat the soup. All we could hear was a rough noise.

“I remember the name of the programme,” she said. “Perhaps we can find it online.” I searched and found a recording. We listened to the last part again. Grandma added the missing time to her notes: fifteen minutes, not fifty.

The following morning, I helped her prepare the vegetables. She cut the carrots into small pieces and asked me to measure the water. I almost poured it straight into the pot. “Use the jug,” she said. “We need to know the amount.” The marks on its side showed the number of millilitres.

While the soup was heating, Grandma told me that she used to follow recipes from magazines. Radio was useful, but written instructions were easier to consult while cooking. I suggested printing the online recipe. She agreed, provided that we used a large font so she could read it without her glasses.

When we tasted the soup, we both found it too salty. I felt the whole morning had been wasted, but Grandma laughed. “We have a meal, and we know what to change.” She crossed out “one spoon of salt” and wrote “half a spoon” in its place. Then she dated the page. The recipe was no longer an order we had to follow exactly. It was a starting point for a meal that would suit us.
